title: Talking about ideas: abstract nouns
goal: Build and recognise the abstract nouns that carry serious conversation (keindahan, kesulitan, pembangunan, perbaikan, pertanian) and use ke-…-an in its other everyday job: saying something is too big, too small or too long.
bekal: turn adjectives into qualities with ke-…-an: *indah, keindahan; sulit, kesulitan*
turn verbs into processes and fields with pe-…-an and per-…-an: *pembangunan, perbaikan, pertanian*
complain politely that something does not fit: *kekecilan, kepanjangan, kesempitan*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Survei di sawah
dialogs.intro: Mid-March 2028. For the project's baseline survey, Sarah and Yoga walk out to the rice fields to interview Pak Darto, a farmer in his sixties, in his little field hut.

notes: **Para petani.** *Para* marks a group of people, rather like "the" + plural: *para petani* (the farmers), *para tamu* (the guests), *para ibu*. It is formal and only for people. ⚠️ Do not add reduplication too: ✗ *para petani-petani*.

**Kemarau and musim hujan.** Java has two seasons: *musim kemarau* (dry, roughly April to October) and *musim hujan* (wet, roughly November to March). Farmers plan everything around them, and so does tourism: the rice fields are greenest just after the rains begin.

**Kekurangan and kebanjiran** are the adversative ke-…-an from A2: something bad happens to the subject. *Sawah kekurangan air* (the fields suffer a lack of water), *Desa kami kebanjiran* (our village got flooded). Same shape as the abstract nouns in this unit, different job; the sentence tells you which.

**Justru** — "precisely, on the contrary, actually it's the reverse". It corrects an assumption: Pak Darto fears hotels, Yoga says it is *precisely* the fields they want. Unit 9 looks at it closely; for now, notice that both Yoga and Sarah use it to turn an objection round.

**Lha, nggih, wong.** Three Javanese touches in Pak Darto's Indonesian. *Lha* is "well, now" at the start of a reaction; *nggih* is the polite Javanese "yes", used here as a soft "mind you"; *wong* means "person, people", as in *wong kota* (city people). You will hear all three all over Central Java.

**Tandur** is Javanese for transplanting rice seedlings by hand, walking backwards through the mud. The Indonesian is *menanam padi*. Village tourism has made *tandur* a small attraction in its own right, and farmers still find that faintly hilarious.

grammars.title: ke-…-an: from a quality to a noun
body: Wrap *ke-…-an* round an adjective (and a few verbs) and you get the abstract noun: the quality itself. It is the Indonesian answer to English *-ness*, *-ity* and *-ty*.
after: The noun behaves like any other: it takes *-nya*, *ini*, adjectives, and it can be the subject. *Keindahannya luar biasa* (its beauty is extraordinary).
💬 Everyday speech often avoids the abstract noun and uses the adjective with *-nya* instead: *susahnya apa?* (what's the hard part?) for *kesulitannya apa?*

grammars.title: pe-…-an and per-…-an: the process and the field
body: *Pe-…-an* is built from a me- verb and names the process or its result. *Per-…-an* is built mostly from ber- verbs and names an activity or a whole domain. The sound changes of pe- follow me- exactly.
after: The quickest test: find the verb. *Membangun* has me-, so the noun is *pembangunan*. *Bertani* has ber-, so it is *pertanian*. *Memperbaiki* has memper-, so the noun keeps *per-*: *perbaikan*.
⚠️ *Penghasilan* is income; *hasil* is result or harvest; *pengalaman* (experience) comes from *mengalami*. All three are about equally common and easy to mix up.

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Kebaya pinjaman
dialogs.intro: The next Saturday. The village is holding its *bersih desa*, a thanksgiving ceremony, on Sunday, and Bu Ratna insists Sarah should wear a kebaya. She has brought one of her own.

notes: **Kebaya and kain.** The *kebaya* is the fitted, often lace or embroidered, blouse; with it a woman wears a *kain* (in Javanese *jarik*), a length of batik wrapped as a skirt, and sometimes a *selendang* (sash). Wearing one to a village ceremony is a gesture of respect, and people will be delighted.

**Monggo dicoba** — literally "please, (it) is tried". Offering something with a passive imperative is very polite in Java: *monggo dimakan*, *silakan diminum*. The guest is not ordered to act; the food, or the kebaya, simply waits to be enjoyed.
**Kayaknya** is the spoken form of *sepertinya* (it seems, I think). Sarah softens her complaint with it. Unit 7 collects all the ways of hedging an opinion; *kayaknya* is the one you will hear most.

**Tidak merepotkan?** — "isn't it troublesome (for you)?" *Merepotkan* means "to cause trouble, to be a bother". Checking that you are not a burden is expected before accepting a favour; the host is then expected to say *tidak*, and usually means it.
**Terharu** means "moved, touched", the feeling when someone's kindness catches you off guard. It is a ter- word of state, no doer. *Saya jadi terharu* uses *jadi* for "it makes me, I end up".

**Ayu, kecantikan, kebanggaan.** *Ayu* is Javanese for pretty, graceful, used freely in Indonesian in Java. *Kecantikan* (beauty, of a person) and *kebanggaan* (pride) are ke-…-an nouns from *cantik* and *bangga*. Note *keindahan* is for places and things, *kecantikan* for people.

grammars.title: ke-…-an meaning "too"
body: With adjectives of size, fit, price and taste, *ke-…-an* has a third job: "too much so, and that's a problem". It is conversational and very common in shops and at the tailor's.
after: This "too" meaning belongs to speech. In writing use *terlalu*. And ⚠️ some of these forms are also abstract nouns: *kebesaran* is "greatness" in *kebesaran Tuhan*, and *kesempitan* is "hardship" in *kesempitan hidup*. Context sorts it out at once.
💬 In Jakarta you will hear *kegedean* (too big, from *gede*) and *kekecilan* side by side.

sections.title: One root, a family of words

blocks.text: Indonesian vocabulary grows in families. Learn one root and you can often guess four more words. Each row below starts from a root and fans out into the person, the verb and the abstract noun.

The family is not always complete, and the meanings drift: *panduan* is a guidebook, not "guidance" in general (that is *bimbingan*). But guessing and then checking in KBBI is exactly how Indonesians themselves learn new formal words.
Newspapers and official speeches are built from these nouns. Recognising them is half of reading a headline. Each of these phrases appeared in the project's first report.

blocks.title: A reading tip
items: Long nouns stack: *pengembangan desa wisata berbasis masyarakat* is "community-based tourism-village development". Read them from the left, and the first noun is the head.
Strip the affixes to find the root: *keberlanjutan* is *ke-* + *ber-lanjut* + *-an*, "the quality of continuing", so sustainability.
When a sentence feels heavy, turn the nouns back into verbs in your head: *pelestarian lingkungan* becomes *melestarikan lingkungan*, to conserve the environment.
